question: Regulation (EU) 2019/1242, as amended by Regulation (EU) 2024/1610, sets unprecedented CO₂ reduction targets for new heavy-duty vehicles: -15 % by 2025, -43 % by 2030, and -64 % by 2035 compared to 2019 levels. However, these targets expose EU manufacturers to significant fines, even though several external factors are preventing the necessary market uptake of zero-emission models.

Only around 3-4 % of new heavy-duty vehicles registered today are zero-emission. The main obstacles are the lack of purchase incentives, the high total cost of ownership and, above all, the absence of a reliable charging and refuelling network across the EU. The targets of the Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation remain insufficient and unevenly implemented by Member States.
Considering this and recalling Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s letter of 20 October 2025 promising concrete measures to assist heavy-duty manufacturers in reaching their targets: 1.
What measures will the Commission adopt to ensure that Member States meet their targets under the Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation for charging and refuelling infrastructure?
What targeted actions will the Commission take to reduce the total cost of ownership for zero-emission vehicles?
What additional measures does the Commission intend to adopt to ensure that manufacturer efforts and zero-emission sales volumes are on track to meet these targets?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.2.2026) Regulation (EU) 2023/1804 on the deployment for alternative fuels infrastructure1 requires Member States to ensure that a minimum of publicly accessible recharging infrastructure dedicated to heavy-duty vehicles (HDV) and hydrogen refuelling infrastructure is deployed along the trans-European transport (TEN-T) network and in urban nodes.

The Commission supports the infrastructure development through the Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Facility2. The Commission will review Regulation (EU) 2023/1804 by the end of 2026 and has started preparatory work for the Impact Assessment that will among others look into the target setting.

Total cost of ownership (TCO) depends on many aspects such as the vehicle purchase cost, road tolls, taxation and energy costs. While the Commission has no power to directly influence the TCO, Member States can use flexibilities under EU legislation to support zero emission heavy duty vehicles.

For example, by exempting zero emission trucks from road tolls as foreseen in Directive 1999/62/EC on the charging of heavy goods vehicles for the use of certain infrastructures3. In addition, European funds such as the Recovery and Resilience Facility4 can be used to support the purchase of zero emission HDV.

The Commission is constantly monitoring the evolution of zero-emission vehicles being registered and assessing the compliance of manufacturers with the targets set by the HDV Standards Regulation 2019/12425.

In addition, it has set up a high-level task force addressing the enabling conditions necessary to meet the 2030 targets, mainly in relation to the financial de-risking and permitting of HDV charging infrastructure.
